title: Prevalence Study and Analysis of Care Quality for Complex Wounds in the University Acute Care Hospital Sector
summary:
Background
The care of people with complex wounds is currently inadequate in Germany and internationally. Particularly in the outpatient setting (e.g., for treatments outside of hospitals), there is uncertainty about how care can be effectively organized in the future. Hospitals, especially university hospitals, could play a key role in closing these gaps in care. Reliable data is needed to better assess this situation.

Research Question
The study investigates how frequently wounds occur in patients at a university hospital and how they are treated. To this end, data will be collected on how many of the participants have a wound and how many do not. Additionally, the study aims to better understand how wounds develop, how long they have existed, how they are treated, and which processes play a role in this. The goal is to improve the long-term care of people with wounds.

Methodology (Study Procedure)
In 2026, a sample of 300 randomly selected patients at a university hospital will be examined. Both individuals with and without wounds will be included.

The study will collect various data, such as: general personal information (e.g., age, gender), information about the wound (type, size, healing process), existing medical conditions and treatments, as well as the processes involved in medical and nursing care.

All data will be treated confidentially.

For chronic wounds, individual treatment courses are also described in greater detail to identify typical patterns and improve care in the future. Here, too, all data is processed in such a way that the participants cannot be identified.

Objective of the study
The findings are intended to help improve the care of people with wounds in the long term and to better plan future treatment structures.
conditions: This study focuses on patients with acute and chronic wounds. In this context, a wound is defined as any loss of the barrier between the skin and the external environment, and thus the destruction of tissue on the body’s external surfaces (Dissemond & Kröger, 2020). This includes erosions and ulcerations of any origin, regardless of their duration and type of wound healing (primary or secondary) .  Internal ulcerations—that is, tissue damage to internal body surfaces—are not of interest. In this study, erosions are defined as wounds of the epidermis (Dissemond & Kröger, 2020). Ulcerations are therefore wounds whose damage extends beyond the epidermis (Dissemond & Kröger, 2020). Wounds are classified as chronic if they have not healed within eight weeks or if there are underlying conditions requiring treatment, such as in the case of vascular ulcers (arterial, venous, or mixed leg ulcers), pressure ulcers, and ulcers associated with diabetes mellitus (Dissemond & Kröger, 2020). This classification is also applied when data collectors suspect the presence of the aforementioned underlying conditions. Accordingly, all wounds that do not meet the above definition and have therefore developed recently are classified as acute (Dissemond & Kröger, 2020).  Translated with DeepL.com (free version)

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
The study population generally includes all patients at the university hospital, regardless of their underlying medical conditions or the reason for their treatment.
Exclusion criteria:
However, for reasons of sensitivity, patients who are in the terminal phase of life or who cannot be examined by the research team for other critical reasons (life-threatening or unstable condition; psychosis, isolation, radiation exposure, etc.) are excluded from in-person interviews or examinations.
